title: Auckland removed minimum parking requirements citywide in 2016, and new developments near frequent transit have since provided markedly less parking
oneLiner: The closest large-scale natural experiment in a comparable city.
body: The Auckland Unitary Plan, operative from late 2016, removed minimum parking requirements across the city. Subsequent research found that developments near frequent public transport built substantially fewer spaces per dwelling, while those in car-dependent areas continued to provide roughly what they had before.
contextBackground: Auckland is the reference case for Australian councils because its housing market, car ownership and urban form are similar. It is also the case opponents study for evidence of street-parking spillover.
contextDisagreement: The change in parking provision is well documented. Whether it reduced housing costs, and whether it worsened on-street parking in affected suburbs, are still being argued over.

claimItself.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether planning schemes should stop requiring a set number of car spaces per new dwelling and let builders decide.
claimItself.body: Most Australian planning schemes require new apartments and townhouses to include a minimum number of off-street car spaces, typically one or more per dwelling. The proposal removes the minimum. Developers could still build parking; they would no longer be required to.
